en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 34.1 (SN 34.1, PTS SN iii 263) 1.
The Chapter on Jhāna The Discourse on Attainment Rooted in Concentration (Samādhimūlakasamāpattisutta)
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.
What are the four?
“Here, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in concentration regarding concentration, but not skilled in attainment regarding concentration.
Here, monks, another meditator is skilled in attainment regarding concentration, but not skilled in concentration regarding concentration.
Here, monks, yet another meditator is neither skilled in concentration regarding concentration nor skilled in attainment regarding concentration.”
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is skilled in concentration regarding concentration and skilled in attainment regarding concentration.

In this regard, monks, that meditator who is skilled in concentration regarding concentration and skilled in attainment regarding concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the supreme, and the most sublime among these four types of meditators."
“Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk, from milk curds, from curds butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee—
which is declared to be the best among them— so too, monks, that meditator who is skilled in concentration and skilled in the attainment of concentration is the foremost,
the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among these four types of meditators.”
First.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 34.2 (SN 34.2, PTS SN iii 264) 1.
The Chapter on Jhāna (Jhānavagga)
The Discourse on the Foundation of Concentration.
Setting at Sāvatthī:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.”
Which four?
Here, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in concentration regarding concentration, but not skilled in stability regarding concentration.
And here, monks, another meditator is skilled in stability regarding concentration, but not skilled in concentration regarding concentration.
"But here, monks, a certain meditator is neither skilled in concentration nor skilled in steadiness in concentration.
Yet here, monks, another meditator is both skilled in concentration and skilled in steadiness in concentration.

Among these four types of meditators, monks, the one who is skilled in concentration and skilled in steadiness in concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime."
“Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk, from milk curds, from curds butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee—

which is declared to be the best among them— so too, monks, that meditator who is skilled in concentration and skilled in stability in concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among these four types of meditators. This is the second [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 34.3 (SN 34.3, PTS SN iii 265) 1. Jhānavagga Samādhimūlakavuṭṭhānasutta: The Discourse on Emerging from Concentration Rooted in Concentration At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliant; when his mind is pliant, he attains the ability to emerge at will from that concentration. “Just as, bhikkhus, when a bowl of water is settled and undisturbed, one can see one’s own face reflected therein; so too, when a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliant; when his mind is pliant, he attains the ability to emerge at will from that concentration. “When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has emerged from that concentration, he recollects it thus: ‘That was the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, which I, having been secluded, entered and dwelt in; that was the rapture and pleasure born of concentration, which I, having attained unification of mind, entered and dwelt in; that was the pleasure of tranquility, which I, having gained mental serenity, entered and dwelt in; that was the equanimity of relinquishment, which I, having abandoned desire, entered and dwelt in. “This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who emerges from concentration rooted in concentration.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators. What are the four? [Text continues...]"
“Here, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in concentration regarding concentration, but not skilled in emerging from concentration.
Here, monks, another meditator is skilled in emerging from concentration regarding concentration, but not skilled in concentration regarding concentration.
Here, monks, yet another meditator is neither skilled in concentration regarding concentration nor skilled in emerging from concentration.”
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is skilled in concentration and skilled in emerging from concentration.

Among these four types of meditators, monks, this one who is skilled in concentration and skilled in emerging from concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime.
Just as, monks, milk comes from a cow... [and so on].
"And he is preeminent.
Third.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 34.4 (SN 34.4, PTS SN iii 265)
1. The Chapter on Jhānas.
The Discourse on the Well-Developed [Mind] Rooted in Concentration.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain meditator is skilled in concentration regarding concentration, but not skilled in steadiness in concentration.”
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is skilled in steadying the mind in concentration, but not skilled in mastery over concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in mastery over concentration nor skilled in steadying the mind in concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in mastery over concentration and skilled in steadying the mind in concentration."

In this regard, monks, that meditator who is skilled in concentration and skilled in making concentration pliable is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the supreme, and the most sublime among these four types of meditators.
Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk...
[and so on] ...the most sublime.”
The Fourth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 34.5 (SN 34.5, PTS SN iii 266) 1.
The Chapter on Jhāna (Jhānavagga)
The Discourse on the Foundation of Concentration as the Object.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.”
Which four?
Here, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in concentration regarding concentration, but not skilled in the object of concentration.
But here, monks, another meditator is skilled in the object of concentration regarding concentration, but not skilled in concentration regarding concentration.
"But here, monks, a certain meditator is neither skilled in concentration regarding concentration, nor is he skilled in the object regarding concentration.
Here, monks, a certain meditator is both skilled in concentration regarding concentration and skilled in the object regarding concentration.

Among these four types of meditators, monks, this one who is skilled in concentration regarding concentration and skilled in the object regarding concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the supreme, and the most eminent."
“Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk … [and so on] … and the cream is the most excellent.
The fifth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 34.6 (SN 34.6, PTS SN iii 266) 1. Jhānavagga Samādhimūlakagocarasutta: The Discourse on the Range Based on Concentration “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliable; when his mind is pliable, he attains the range of the mind that is based on concentration. And what is the range of the mind that is based on concentration? ‘May my body be thus,’ and it becomes so for him; ‘May my body be thus otherwise,’ and it becomes so for him. This is called the range of the mind that is based on concentration. When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliable; when his mind is pliable, he attains this range of the mind that is based on concentration.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators. Which four?
“Here, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in concentration regarding concentration, but not skilled in the range of concentration.
Here, monks, another meditator is skilled in the range of concentration regarding concentration, but not skilled in concentration regarding concentration.
Here, monks, yet another meditator is neither skilled in concentration regarding concentration nor skilled in the range of concentration regarding concentration.”
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is skilled in concentration and skilled in the domain of concentration.

Among these four types of meditators, monks, this one who is skilled in concentration and skilled in the domain of concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the supreme, and the most sublime.
Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk... [and so on].
“And excellent.
The sixth [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 34.7 (SN 34.7, PTS SN iii 267).
1. The Chapter on Jhāna.
Discourse on the Aspiration Rooted in Concentration.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators. What four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain meditator is skilled in concentration regarding concentration, but is not skilled in the directing of concentration.
“Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is skilled in the directing of concentration, but not skilled in concentration itself.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in concentration itself nor skilled in the directing of concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in concentration itself and skilled in the directing of concentration.”

"In this regard, monks, that meditator who is skilled in concentration and skilled in the directing of concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among these four types of meditators.
Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk...
[and so on] ...so too is he the most sublime."
The Seventh.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 34.8 (SN 34.8, PTS SN iii 267) 1.
The Chapter on Jhāna (Jhānavagga)
The Discourse on the One Who Acts with Care Based on Concentration.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.”
What are the four?
Here, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in concentration regarding concentration, but he does not practice it with thorough care.
And here, monks, another meditator practices with thorough care regarding concentration, but he is not skilled in concentration regarding concentration.
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in concentration nor does he practice concentration with diligence.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in concentration and practices concentration with diligence.

Among these four types of meditators, monks, that meditator who is both skilled in concentration and practices concentration with diligence is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime."
“Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk … [and so on] … and the cream of the cream.
The eighth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 34.9 (SN 34.9, PTS SN iii 268) 1. Jhānavagga Samādhimūlakasātaccakārīsutta (The Discourse on One Who Acts with Persistence Rooted in Concentration) “Bhikkhus, when one dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardently, clearly comprehending, and mindfully, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, then, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. If, while he dwells thus, he acts with persistence, exerts himself, and applies his mind, then he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through this very seclusion, this very detachment, this very relinquishment, and this very abandonment, he attains final knowledge in this very life. This, bhikkhus, is the second fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now, more excellent than the former. Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the subsiding of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without thought and examination, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration. If, while he dwells thus, he acts with persistence, exerts himself, and applies his mind, then he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through this very seclusion, this very detachment, this very relinquishment, and this very abandonment, he attains final knowledge in this very life. This, bhikkhus, is the third fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now, more excellent than the former. Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. If, while he dwells thus, he acts with persistence, exerts himself, and applies his mind, then he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through this very seclusion, this very detachment, this very relinquishment, and this very abandonment, he attains final knowledge in this very life. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now, more excellent than the former. Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. If, while he dwells thus, he acts with persistence, exerts himself, and applies his mind, then he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through this very seclusion, this very detachment, this very relinquishment, and this very abandonment, he attains final knowledge in this very life. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now, more excellent than the former.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators. Which four?
In this case, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in concentration regarding concentration, but does not practice with persistence in concentration.
In this case, however, monks, a certain meditator practices with persistence in concentration, but is not skilled in concentration regarding concentration.
In this case, however, monks, a certain meditator is neither skilled in concentration regarding concentration nor does he practice with persistence in concentration.
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in concentration and persistent in his practice of concentration.

Among these four types of meditators, monks, this one who is skilled in concentration and persistent in his practice of concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime.
Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk... [and so on].
“And he is preeminent.
The ninth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 34.10 (SN 34.10, PTS SN iii 268).
1. The Chapter on Jhāna.
Discourse on Engaging in What is Suitable Based on Concentration.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain meditator is skilled in concentration, but not one who practices what is conducive to concentration.”
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator acts in a way that is conducive to concentration, but he is not skilled in concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in concentration nor does he act in a way that is conducive to concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in concentration and acts in a way that is conducive to concentration."

In this regard, monks, that meditator who is skilled in concentration and practices what is conducive to concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among these four types of meditators.
Just as, monks, milk comes from a cow...
[and so on] ...so is he the most sublime.”
The Tenth.
(Based on Concentration.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 34.11 (SN 34.11, PTS SN iii 269)
1. The Chapter on Jhānas.
Discourse on the Stability Based on Attainment.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain meditator is skilled in attaining concentration, but not skilled in remaining in concentration.”
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is skilled in the maintenance of concentration, but not skilled in the attainment of concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in the attainment of concentration nor skilled in the maintenance of concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in the attainment of concentration and skilled in the maintenance of concentration."

"In this regard, monks, among these four types of meditators, the one who is skilled both in attaining concentration and in remaining established in concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime of them all.
Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk...
[and so on] ...so too is he the most sublime."
Eleventh.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 34.12 (SN 34.12, PTS SN iii 269) 1.
The Chapter on Jhāna (Jhānavagga)
The Discourse on Emerging from Attainment Based on Jhāna.
At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of meditators.”
Which four?
Here, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in attaining concentration, but not skilled in emerging from concentration.
But here, monks, another meditator is skilled in emerging from concentration, but not skilled in attaining concentration.
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in attaining concentration nor skilled in emerging from concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in attaining concentration and skilled in emerging from concentration.
Of these, monks, as for the meditator who... [and so on].
"And excellent.
The twelfth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 34.13 (SN 34.13, PTS SN iii 270)
1. The Chapter on Jhānas.
The Discourse on the Delightful [State] Rooted in Attainment.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain meditator is skilled in attaining concentration, but not skilled in maintaining concentration.
“Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is skilled in steadying his mind in concentration, but not skilled in attaining concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in attaining concentration nor skilled in steadying his mind in concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in attaining concentration and skilled in steadying his mind in concentration.”
Therein... [as before] ...and it is excellent. Thus ends the thirteenth [chapter].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 34.14 (SN 34.14, PTS SN iii 270) 1. Jhānavagga Samāpattimūlakaārammaṇasutta (The Discourse on the Object Based on Attainment) “Bhikkhus, when the mind is concentrated, it knows as it really is: ‘This is suffering. When the mind is concentrated, it knows as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. When the mind is concentrated, it knows as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. When the mind is concentrated, it knows as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. When the mind is concentrated, bhikkhus, one understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering. When the mind is concentrated, one understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. When the mind is concentrated, one understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. When the mind is concentrated, one understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will develop concentration; we will cultivate concentration. It is in this way that you should train yourselves.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four meditators. Which four?
In this case, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in attaining concentration, but not skilled in the object of concentration.
In this case, however, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in the object of concentration, but not skilled in attaining concentration.
In this case, however, monks, a certain meditator is neither skilled in attaining concentration nor skilled in the object of concentration.
"But here, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in attaining concentration and skilled in the object of concentration.
In that regard...
[as before] ...he is preeminent."
The Fourteenth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 34.15 (SN 34.15, PTS SN iii 270) 1.
The Chapter on Jhāna (Jhānavagga)
The Discourse on the Range Based on Attainment.
Setting at Sāvatthī:
"Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of meditators."
Which four?
Here, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in attaining concentration, but not skilled in the range of concentration.
And here, monks, another meditator is skilled in the range of concentration, but not skilled in attaining concentration.
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in the attainment of concentration nor skilled in the range of concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in the attainment of concentration and skilled in the range of concentration. In that case... [and so forth].
“And excellent.
The fifteenth [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 34.16 (SN 34.16, PTS SN iii 271)
1. The Chapter on Jhāna.
Discourse on the Aspiration Based on Attainment.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain meditator is skilled in attaining concentration, but not skilled in directing the mind within concentration.”
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is skilled in directing his mind toward concentration, but not skilled in attaining concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in attaining concentration nor skilled in directing his mind toward concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in attaining concentration and skilled in directing his mind toward concentration."
Therein...
[and so on] ...and he is preeminent.
The sixteenth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 34.17 (SN 34.17, PTS SN iii 271) 1. Jhānavagga Samāpattimūlakasakkaccasutta "Monks, when a bhikkhu is diligent in the attainment of the first jhāna, he is diligent in what is wholesome; when he is diligent in the attainment of the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna, he is diligent in what is wholesome. When a bhikkhu is diligent in the attainment of the base of infinite space, he is diligent in what is wholesome; when he is diligent in the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness... the base of nothingness... the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he is diligent in what is wholesome. When a bhikkhu is diligent in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he is diligent in what is wholesome."
At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.
What are the four?
"In this case, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in attaining concentration, but not one who practices concentration with diligence.
In this case, monks, another meditator is one who practices concentration with diligence, but not one who is skilled in attaining concentration.
In this case, monks, yet another meditator is neither skilled in attaining concentration nor one who practices concentration with diligence."
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in attaining concentration and one who practices concentration with thorough care.
In that regard...
[as before] ...he is preeminent."
The Seventeenth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 34.18 (SN 34.18, PTS SN iii 271) 1.
The Chapter on Jhāna (Jhānavagga)
The Discourse on Constant Perseverance Rooted in Attainment.
Setting: Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators."
Which four?
Here, monks, a certain meditator is skilled in attaining concentration, but not one who practices concentration with persistence.
And here, monks, another meditator is one who practices concentration with persistence, but not one who is skilled in attaining concentration.
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in attaining concentration nor is he one who practices with persistence in concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in attaining concentration and one who practices with persistence in concentration.
In that regard... [and so on].
“And he is preeminent.
The eighteenth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 34.19 (SN 34.19, PTS SN iii 271)
1. The Chapter on Jhānas:
Discourse on Doing What is Beneficial Based on Attainment.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain meditator is skilled in attaining concentration, but not skilled in acting in a way that is conducive to concentration.”
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator acts in a way that is conducive to concentration, but is not skilled in attaining concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is neither skilled in attaining concentration nor does he act in a way that is conducive to concentration.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain meditator is both skilled in attaining concentration and acts in a way that is conducive to concentration."

In this regard, monks, that meditator who is both skilled in attaining concentration and one who acts in a way conducive to concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among these four types of meditators.
Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk, from milk curds, from curds butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee— which is declared to be the foremost— so too, monks,
that meditator who is skilled in attaining concentration and acts in a way conducive to concentration...
"And this one who practices what is suitable is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among these four meditators.
(The nineteenth [section].
Based on Attainment.)

Saṃyutta Nikāya 34.20–27 (SN 34.20, PTS SN iii 272) 1. Jhānavagga The Octad on Emergence Based on Stability, etc. (20) “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, he directs it toward the base of the infinity of space; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is concentrated, whose mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, who has directed it toward the base of the infinity of space, who has mastered it, and who dwells having realized it with his body. (21) “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, he directs it toward the base of the infinity of consciousness; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is concentrated, whose mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, who has directed it toward the base of the infinity of consciousness, who has mastered it, and who dwells having realized it with his body. (22) “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, he directs it toward the base of nothingness; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is concentrated, whose mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, who has directed it toward the base of nothingness, who has mastered it, and who dwells having realized it with his body. (23) “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, he directs it toward the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is concentrated, whose mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, who has directed it toward the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, who has mastered it, and who dwells having realized it with his body. (24) “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, he directs it toward the cessation of perception and feeling; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is concentrated, whose mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, who has directed it toward the cessation of perception and feeling, who has mastered it, and who dwells having realized it with his body. (25) “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, he directs it toward the base of the infinity of space; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. Having emerged from that, he directs it toward the base of the infinity of consciousness; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. Having emerged from that, he directs it toward the base of nothingness; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. Having emerged from that, he directs it toward the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. Having emerged from that, he directs it toward the cessation of perception and feeling; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is concentrated, whose mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, who has directed it toward the base of the infinity of space... [and so on] ...who has directed it toward the cessation of perception and feeling, who has mastered it, and who dwells having realized it with his body. (26) “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is concentrated, his mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, he directs it toward the base of the infinity of space;

having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. Having emerged from that, he directs it toward the base of the infinity of consciousness; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. Having emerged from that, he directs it toward the base of nothingness; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. Having emerged from that, he directs it toward the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. Having emerged from that, he directs it toward the cessation of perception and feeling; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. Then, having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is concentrated, whose mind is pliant, malleable, and luminous, who has directed it toward the base of the infinity of space... Having emerged from that, he directs it toward the cessation of perception and feeling; having mastered it, he dwells having realized it with his body. "Bhikkhus, there are these four types of meditators.
What are the four?
"Here, monks, a certain meditator is constant in concentration, but not one who practices what is suitable for concentration.
Here, monks, another meditator practices what is suitable for concentration, but is not constant in concentration.
Here, monks, yet another meditator is neither constant in concentration nor one who practices what is suitable for concentration."
"But here, monks, a certain meditator is both constant in his practice toward concentration and practices what is conducive to concentration.

In this regard, monks, that meditator who is both constant in his practice toward concentration and practices what is conducive to concentration is declared to be the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among these four types of meditators.
Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk, from milk curd, from curd butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee—which is declared to be the very pinnacle."

“In the same way, monks, that meditator who is both constant in concentration and practices what is conducive to concentration is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the supreme, and the most sublime among these four types of meditators.
